ekg-sequence: How fast does the EKG sequence grow, where each number is the smallest unused one sharing a prime factor with the one before? Building on Tomer Haver's work, we prove the formula Lagarias, Rains and Sloane predicted in 2002 at almost all positions, with a computer-checked proof.
uniform-5-polytopes: Uniform polytopes are higher-dimensional cousins of the Archimedean solids; is the known list of the dent-free ones in five dimensions complete, as it is in four? We prove that it is, with a computer-assisted proof.
steinberg-c4-c9: If a flat network with no crossings has no rings of four or nine distinct points, can it always be colored with three colors so that linked points differ? We show not, with an 82-point example and a computer-checked proof.
stanley-smith-forms: Sums of swaps of objects act on standard tables of whole numbers; is Richard Stanley's 2016 formula for the list of numbers summarizing each such action right? We show it fails, already for five objects, with a counterexample checked by computer.
stanley-class-sum-snf: What standard list of numbers summarizes multiplying sums of rearrangements, grouped by cycle shape, by the sum of all ways to cycle the objects around one loop, as Richard Stanley asked in 2019? We find it for every number of objects, confirming Stanley's two conjectured cases, with a computer-checked proof.
ekg-bounds: In the EKG sequence, where each number is the smallest unused one sharing a prime factor with the one before, is a term's ratio to its position largest at term 7 and smallest at term 28, as conjectured in 2002? Building on Tomer Haver's work, we prove it, with a computer-assisted proof.
locally-toroidal-polytopes: For which grid sizes do certain abstract four-dimensional shapes, built from square grids wrapped onto doughnuts, exist? For one family Schulte and Weiss asked about in 2006, we prove they exist for every pair of different odd sizes, with a computer-checked proof; their finiteness and symmetries stay open.
locked-trominoes: Which rectangles can be tiled by three-square pieces so that no two pieces can be re-cut into two different three-square pieces? We prove Jamie Tucker-Foltz's conjecture, completing the answer: both sides at least four and area divisible by three, with a computer-checked proof.
pseudostandard-attractors: Some strings of 0s and 1s grow by repeatedly extending a word into its mirror image, possibly with 0s and 1s swapped; do four marked spots always suffice to touch a copy of every stretch of each such word, as conjectured in 2023? We give a computer-assisted counterexample of length 36.
scattering-coefficients: Scattering diagrams are patterns of rays, each labeled with numbers, that underlie a branch of algebra; does a 2024 conjectured formula of Elgin, Reading and Stella give one ray's numbers? We prove it does, with a computer-checked proof.
monotone-query-gap: For a yes-or-no rule on fair coin flips, where switching an input on never switches the answer off, is reading inputs one at a time ever costlier on average than the best split into fixed-answer cases? We show it can be, with a five-input example and a computer-assisted proof.
multitwist-exceptions: Twisting a surface along a loop, then applying a fixed motion, gives a thoroughly mixing map except at a few consecutive twist counts; with twists along several loops, must the exceptions stay that close together? On a five-holed sphere we show they can be arbitrarily far apart, with a written proof, partly computer-checked.
lit-only-sigma: In a lights game, pressing a point of a network flips its neighbors; if banning presses on unlit points can raise the fewest lights reachable from some start by more than half the number of points, must the network be of one very regular kind? We give counterexamples, with a computer-checked proof.
cubelike-cospectrality: Networks built on strings of 0s and 1s can hold groups of points that behave alike, up to sign, in every natural vibration pattern; is a known size limit on such groups always reached? In dimension seven the largest has four points, not eight, by a computer-assisted proof.
game-grundy-gap: In a game where players take turns coloring a network's points, linked points differing, does a greedy version, where every move takes the smallest allowed color, never need more colors? We give a network needing six instead of five, with a computer-assisted proof.
weak-parking: For symmetry groups made of mirror reflections, do two so-called parking spaces carry matching symmetries, as Armstrong, Reiner and Rhoades conjectured in 2012? Two exceptional groups were left; we settle both with a computer-assisted proof, completing the weaker form of the conjecture.
coinvariant-lefschetz: Does an algebraic object attached to every symmetry group of complex reflections have a strong regularity property, as Wachi asked in 2013? One exceptional group was left; we settle it with a computer-assisted proof, completing the answer for all such groups.
noncrossing-symmetric-chains: Can certain families of noncrossing groupings, attached to a broad class of reflection groups, always be split into chains placed symmetrically between bottom and top, as Henri Mühle asked in 2015? We settle the remaining cases with a computer-assisted proof; a stronger question stays open.
complex-parking: Armstrong, Reiner and Rhoades asked in 2012 whether a comparison of two parking spaces built from mirror-reflection groups extends to complex reflection groups. For the basic well-behaved groups and simplest setting, after correcting a convention, we add the last missing case to earlier work, with a written proof and computer checks.
lned-counterexample: Do certain operations on polynomials always turn an ideal, a family closed under multiplying by any polynomial, into a set with a special closure property, as Wenhua Zhao conjectured? Using Zhao's own criterion, we show not for shift differences in one variable, with a computer-checked proof.
matrix-lfed-counterexample: Do certain operations on algebras always produce sets with a special closure property, as Wenhua Zhao conjectured in 2017? Using the same triangular-matrix idea as Zongmin Liu, we give one counterexample for both operations where the order of multiplication matters, with a computer-checked proof.
cameron-donkin: Start with a prime and keep appending the smallest prime factor of one plus the product of all terms so far; can a well-chosen start keep 3 out of any number of first terms, as Steve Donkin asked? We prove so, with a computer-checked proof; keeping 3 out forever stays open.
makonzi-invariants: Do three basic equations explain every relation among certain polynomials read off a three-armed diagram of arrows, as Brian Makonzi conjectured in 2025? We prove so for all arm lengths of at least two, over the complex numbers, with a computer-checked proof.
cocircuit-diameter-counterexample: When flat walls through a point cut up space, the directions along the lines where they meet form a network; can two be further apart than Fukuda and Terlaky's proposed limit? We give 80 walls in 41 dimensions needing at least 42 steps where 41 are allowed, with the key calculation computer-checked.
tight-cycle-c5-turan: How large a share of all triples from many points can be chosen without five points in a ring whose consecutive triples are all chosen? We prove that Mubayi and Rödl's 2002 construction, about 46 percent, is best in the limit, as conjectured, with a computer-checked proof.
sts-broken-spectrum: A Steiner triple system groups points in threes so that any two points share one group; if the points of every group show exactly two colors, can the possible numbers of colors skip a value? We give a 39-point example allowing three or five colors but not four, with a computer-assisted proof.
golden-rado: If 1, 2, 3 and onward get two colors, 1 getting the first and the second never twice in a row, how far until some simple equation must have a one-colored solution? Brian Hopkins's 2021 formula was known to fail in some cases; we prove all others, by a computer-checked proof.
pentagon-tetrads: Can four identical pentagons be placed without overlap so that each pair shares a stretch of border, leaving no hole? We prove they cannot, so six sides is the fewest for tiles of this kind, with a computer-assisted proof.
spinning-switches: In a spinning-switches puzzle, an adversary secretly rearranges hidden switches after each move; when can a fixed move sequence surely pass every setting? Building on Peter Kagey's work, we prove: for finite puzzles under mild conditions, exactly when the numbers of switch states and of rearrangements are powers of one prime, by a computer-checked proof.
queueing-polynomial-convexity: Sending copies of a job to several servers can cut waiting; in a 2020 queueing model of Brosch, Laurent and Steenkamp, is a load formula's value for a blend of two server-choice rules at most the weighted average of theirs? We prove so in every size, with a computer-checked proof.
acyclic-root-extrema: A certain polynomial counts ways to pick points of a network whose links form no closed loop; does one proposed network always have the lowest real solution and the solution farthest from zero for its size? We answer no to both with a twelve-point network and a computer-checked proof.
maximal-matching-logconcavity: When pairing points of a network along links until no more pairs fit, is the count of pairings of each size, squared, always at least the product of the counts for one pair fewer and one more? We give a 76-point network where it is not, with a computer-assisted proof.
ft23-pqd-pmi: Copulas describe how two random quantities depend on each other; do two notions of positive dependence agree for a common family of them, as Fuchs and Tschimpke conjectured in 2023? We give a member with the first kind but not the second, with a computer-checked proof.
zero-forcing-unimodality: In zero forcing, a colored point colors its single uncolored neighbor; counted by size, do the starting sets that color a whole network always rise then fall in number? Using Xinjun Wang's method, we answer no with a 73-point network and a computer-assisted proof.
cd13-universal-dynamics: In a network with no feedback loops, each site updates from the sites it points to; does a known list of algebraic rules describe exactly which update orders always agree, as Collina and D'Andrea asked? We prove so for every finite such network, using finitely many states per site, by a computer-checked proof.
independent-monophonic-ng: One kind of coloring makes linked points differ and avoids three same-colored points on a shortcut-free path; are the colors needed for a network and for its complement, linking exactly the unlinked pairs, at most one more than its point count? We give 21 points needing at least 23, with a computer-assisted proof.
geneson-continuous-gluing: If two point patterns are joined corner to corner into one, is the largest area in a square avoiding stretched copies of the combined pattern at most the sum for each alone, as Jesse Geneson asked in 2021? We prove it is, with a computer-checked proof.
semidistrim-rowmotion: Rowmotion is a natural way of shuffling certain ordered structures called lattices; do two simple conditions pin it down on every finite semidistrim lattice, as Colin Defant and Nathan Williams asked in 2021? We prove they do, with a computer-checked proof.
planar-graceful-coloring: A graceful coloring gives linked points different colors from 1 to 4, with distinct color differences along each point's links; how hard is it to decide whether a flat network has one? Using Bonnet, Chakraborty and Duron's work, we prove it is among the hardest quickly checkable problems, with a written proof, partly computer-checked.
base-r-ehrhart: Counting grid points in or on ever larger copies of a shape gives a polynomial; is it free of negative coefficients for a family of triangle-like shapes built from number bases, as Liam Solus's computations suggested? We show the five-dimensional base-14 one is not, with a computer-checked proof.
baxter-chord-diagrams: A chord diagram joins points on a line in pairs by arcs; are diagrams of one special kind as numerous as Baxter permutations, a well-studied family of orderings, with one fewer entry than the diagram has arcs? We prove Lukas Nabergall's conjecture that they are, with an explicit matching and a computer-checked proof.
random-hitting-set-greedy: To pick few columns of a random sparse 0-and-1 table so every row has a 1 in one of them, does the greedy method approach a standard lower limit as tables grow, as conjectured in 2023? With leftmost or random tie-breaking, we show not, by a computer-checked proof.
iterated-plethysm: Plethysm plugs symmetric polynomials into each other; do certain coefficients of repeated plethysms of the simplest ones always read the same backward as forward, as Gutiérrez and Rosas asked in 2022? We prove they do, with a computer-checked proof.
hamiltonian-degree-sequences: A Hamilton cycle is a round trip through a network of one-way links that visits every point once; do conditions on how many links enter and leave the points guarantee one, as conjectured in 2008? We show they fail from seven points on and hold below, with a computer-assisted proof.
interval-hales-jewett: Coloring all long words over an alphabet always creates a one-colored line of words; can a coloring force each such line to vary its letters in many separate stretches? With two colors, we show the stretches forced can grow with the square of the alphabet size, by a computer-checked proof.
kreweras-cyclic-sieving: Chains of noncrossing partitions attached to Weyl groups, a kind of symmetry group, carry a natural rotation; do certain polynomials count the chains each rotation fixes, as Reiner and Sommers conjectured in 2016? We prove the five exceptional cases by a computer-assisted proof, completing it for every irreducible Weyl group.
harborth-constant: On a square grid with an odd prime side whose coordinates wrap around like a clock, must any distinct points numbering one less than twice the side include a side's worth adding to zero? We prove it for every prime from 11 on, settling the open cases, with a computer-checked proof.
near-equal-budgets: When buyers who value bundles by adding item values share goods that cannot be split, do nearly equal budgets always allow prices at which everything sells and each buyer gets a best affordable bundle? Two buyers always can; three can fail arbitrarily close to equal budgets, by a computer-assisted proof.
hayashi-conjecture: Quandles are algebraic structures used to tell knots apart; in every finite connected one, is a basic shuffle's longest cycle a multiple of its other cycle lengths, as Chuichiro Hayashi conjectured in 2013? We give examples of sizes 1890 and 5670 where it is not, by a written proof that programs recheck.
parallelepiped-triangulation: Can every slanted box with corners on a grid be cut into the smallest possible grid triangles' higher-dimensional cousins, as asked in 2017? We show not, in four and all higher dimensions, with a written proof whose finite steps a short program rechecks.
reptile-simplex: Can a four-dimensional triangle-like shape be cut into a square number of identical smaller copies of itself, other than a fourth power, as asked in 2016? Using a subdivision by Anna Felikson and Pavel Tumarkin, we show one splits into four, with a computer-assisted proof.
abc-front-speedup: When a reaction front spreads through a fluid stirred by a standard model of chaotic flow, does its speed eventually grow in proportion to the stirring strength, as Xin, Yu and Zlatoš asked? For the standard reaction model we prove it does, in every direction, by a written proof, partly computer-checked.
pentagon-billiard-periods: A billiard ball in a regular pentagon can follow a repeating path; does every even number of bounces before repeating, except 2, 12, 14 and 18, occur for a path that no turn of the pentagon preserves? We prove it does, with a written proof, partly computer-checked.
postlie-perfect-nilpotent: Lie algebras are algebraic systems that capture continuous symmetry; can a perfect one and a nilpotent one, two opposite kinds, share one space through a post-Lie structure, as Burde and Dekimpe asked in 2015? Not in finite dimensions, for nonzero perfect ones where adding 1 repeatedly never returns to zero, by a written proof, partly computer-checked.
heawood-family-mu5: The Colin de Verdière number measures a network's topological complexity; are the 78 Heawood-family networks all the minimal ones scoring above five, as proposed in 2006? We give two networks scoring six that cannot be reduced to any of them by deleting or shrinking links, with a computer-assisted proof.
heawood-family-four-flat: A network is 4-flat if gluing a disk onto each of its loops gives a shape that fits in four-dimensional space; are the 78 Heawood-family networks all the minimal ones that fail? We show a known 11-point network is a further minimal failure, with a computer-assisted proof.
game-chromatic-arboricity: If the first player of a coloring game wins with a fixed number of colors on every part of every network in a family, must those networks' links split into boundedly many loop-free pieces, as Xuding Zhu asked? We prove so, with a written proof, partly computer-checked.
pluto-prediscovery: Does Pluto, found in 1930, appear on photographs older than the January 1914 images used for its orbit and the images reported from 1909? On public scans of plates from December 1908 and February 1909 we find faint candidate images for experts to assess, with measurements anyone can rerun.
density-seven: How many seven-letter words over three letters can be chosen with no line, three words identical except at some chosen positions that together show each letter in turn? We prove the answer is 1,302, the size Polymath reached and tentatively conjectured, with a computer-assisted proof.
difference-set-243: On a grid with sides three, nine and nine whose coordinates wrap around like clocks, can 121 points have differences that give each nonzero step exactly 60 times? Keita Baba proved in October 2026 that they cannot; we give an independent computer-assisted proof by a different method.
path-ramsey: If every pair of points is linked and each link gets one of three colors, how many points are needed to force a one-colored chain through ten of them? We prove the answer is 18, as conjectured in 2012, with a computer-checked proof.
thomson-10: How do ten equal electric charges arrange themselves on a ball when they all push each other away? Building on Aravind Karthigeyan's nine-charge proof, we prove that the arrangement long thought best really is the best, and is unique up to rotation and reflection, with a computer-checked proof.
williamson-order-65: Williamson matrices are four tables of plus and minus ones, each made by shifting one row, that fit together exactly; do they exist at size 65, which a 2019 survey called the smallest open size? An exhaustive computer search, which anyone can replay, finds none.
